name: Build BADSHAH AI (APK + AAB)

on:
  workflow_dispatch:
  push:
    branches: [main]
    paths: ["android-app/**", ".github/workflows/android-build.yml"]

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 40
    defaults:
      run:
        working-directory: android-app
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: actions/setup-java@v4
        with: { distribution: temurin, java-version: "17" }

      - uses: gradle/actions/setup-gradle@v4

      # 1) Unit tests (command parser, voice catalog, provider logic)
      - name: Unit tests
        run: ./gradlew --no-daemon testDebugUnitTest

      # 2) Debug APK (always works, signed with the standard Android debug key)
      - name: Assemble debug APK
        run: ./gradlew --no-daemon assembleDebug

      # 3) Release: signed ONLY if you added the 4 secrets + keystore secret (see documentation/BUILD-APK.md).
      - name: Restore release keystore (if secrets exist)
        env:
          KS_B64: ${{ secrets.BADSHAH_KEYSTORE_BASE64 }}
        run: |
          if [ -n "$KS_B64" ]; then
            echo "$KS_B64" | base64 -d > "$RUNNER_TEMP/release.jks"
            echo "BADSHAH_KEYSTORE_FILE=$RUNNER_TEMP/release.jks" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"
            echo "SIGNED=true" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"
          else
            echo "SIGNED=false" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"
            echo "::warning::No keystore secret found: release APK/AAB will be UNSIGNED."
          fi

      - name: Assemble release APK and bundle AAB
        env:
          BADSHAH_KEYSTORE_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.BADSHAH_KEYSTORE_PASSWORD }}
          BADSHAH_KEY_ALIAS: ${{ secrets.BADSHAH_KEY_ALIAS }}
          BADSHAH_KEY_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.BADSHAH_KEY_PASSWORD }}
        run: ./gradlew --no-daemon assembleRelease bundleRelease

      # 4) Verify and name outputs honestly
      - name: Collect + verify artifacts
        run: |
          mkdir -p ../release-artifacts
          D=app/build/outputs/apk/debug/app-debug.apk
          cp "$D" ../release-artifacts/BADSHAH-AI-debug.apk
          if [ "$SIGNED" = "true" ]; then
            cp app/build/outputs/apk/release/app-release.apk ../release-artifacts/BADSHAH-AI-release.apk
            cp app/build/outputs/bundle/release/app-release.aab ../release-artifacts/BADSHAH-AI.aab
          else
            cp app/build/outputs/apk/release/app-release-unsigned.apk ../release-artifacts/BADSHAH-AI-release-UNSIGNED.apk
            cp app/build/outputs/bundle/release/app-release.aab ../release-artifacts/BADSHAH-AI-UNSIGNED.aab
          fi
          BT=$(ls -d "$ANDROID_HOME"/build-tools/* | sort -V | tail -1)
          for f in ../release-artifacts/*.apk; do echo "== $f"; "$BT/apksigner" verify --print-certs "$f" || echo "(not signed / unsigned as expected)"; done
          ls -la ../release-artifacts
          (cd ../release-artifacts && sha256sum * > SHA256SUMS.txt)

      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: BADSHAH-AI-builds
          path: release-artifacts/

# BADSHAH AI: YOUR PERSONAL AI VOICE ASSISTANT

Android assistant (Kotlin, Jetpack Compose, MVVM) + admin website + Supabase backend + Firebase login.

* **AI brain**: Google Gemini and Groq, each user's own key (encrypted on the phone), connection test, model list from the provider, provider switching.
* **Voice**: real installed Android TTS voices (never invented), speed/pitch/style, preview; optional ElevenLabs; speech recognition.
* **Interactive portrait**: your original portrait with idle / listening / thinking / speaking / working / error states, 3D tilt from touch and motion, low-power mode.
* **Phone control** (official intents only, user confirmation for calls/messages): open apps, YouTube, WhatsApp, Chrome, camera, gallery, pick contact, prepare call / WhatsApp / SMS, alarms, timers, web search.
* **Help center** with tickets stored in Supabase, admin replies, optional email.
* **About** page with your images and official social links.
* **Admin panel** at `/admin`: password-only, bcrypt, rate limiting, expiring sessions, analytics, user management, support, app management, security/audit.

Start with **[documentation/INSTALLATION.md](documentation/INSTALLATION.md)**.
What was tested and what was not: **[documentation/TESTING-REPORT.md](documentation/TESTING-REPORT.md)**.

Security rules kept: no API keys in code, no service-role/service-account/keystore secrets in the repo, original photos untouched in `assets/`.

# BADSHAH AI admin panel

Static HTML/CSS/JS (no build step, no third-party scripts, strict CSP).

```
index.html            password-only login (public)
css/admin.css         shared styles (public)
js/api.js, login.js   API client + login (public; never sees the session token)
assets/               logo, favicon
pages/dashboard.html  dashboard shell  } served ONLY to a valid session
pages/js/*.js         dashboard code   } (checked server-side by the Worker)
```
All data comes from `POST /admin/api` → Cloudflare Worker → Supabase Edge Function `admin-api`. See `documentation/ADMIN-GUIDE.md` and `documentation/HOSTING-GUIDE.md`.

    val phone = PhoneExecutor(app)

    }

const val UPDATES_CHANNEL = "badshah_updates"

fun ensureNotificationChannel(nm: NotificationManager) {
    nm.createNotificationChannel(NotificationChannel(UPDATES_CHANNEL, "Support replies & announcements", NotificationManager.IMPORTANCE_DEFAULT))
}

/** Shows push messages (support replies, announcements) while the app is in the foreground. */
class BadshahMessagingService : FirebaseMessagingService() {
    override fun onMessageReceived(message: RemoteMessage) {
        val n = message.notification ?: return
        if (ContextCompat.checkSelfPermission(this, Manifest.permission.POST_NOTIFICATIONS) != PackageManager.PERMISSION_GRANTED) return
        ensureNotificationChannel(getSystemService(NotificationManager::class.java))
        val notif = NotificationCompat.Builder(this, UPDATES_CHANNEL).setSmallIcon(R.drawable.ic_stat_badshah)
            .setContentTitle(n.title ?: getString(R.string.app_name)).setContentText(n.body).setAutoCancel(true).build()
        NotificationManagerCompat.from(this).notify(System.currentTimeMillis().toInt(), notif)
    }
}

/** Everything the assistant can ask the phone to do. Pure data: no Android types. */
sealed class PhoneAction {
    data class OpenApp(val appName: String) : PhoneAction()
    object OpenYouTube : PhoneAction()
    object OpenWhatsApp : PhoneAction()
    object OpenChrome : PhoneAction()
    object OpenCamera : PhoneAction()
    object OpenGallery : PhoneAction()
    object PickContact : PhoneAction()
    data class Call(val target: String) : PhoneAction()
    data class WhatsAppMessage(val target: String, val message: String) : PhoneAction()
    data class Sms(val target: String, val message: String) : PhoneAction()
    data class SetAlarm(val hour24: Int, val minute: Int, val label: String? = null) : PhoneAction()
    data class StartTimer(val seconds: Int, val label: String? = null) : PhoneAction()
    data class WebSearch(val query: String) : PhoneAction()

    /** Calls and messages are never sent silently: the user must confirm first. */
    val needsConfirmation: Boolean
        get() = this is Call || this is WhatsAppMessage || this is Sms
}

/** Framework-free assertions. JUnit wrappers in DomainLogicTest call these; so does the standalone runner. */
object DomainLogic {

    private fun eq(name: String, actual: Any?, expected: Any?) {
        n++; if (actual != expected) failures += "FAIL $name: expected <$expected> got <$actual>" else println("PASS  $name")
    }

        eq("confirm: whatsapp", PhoneAction.WhatsAppMessage("x", "y").needsConfirmation, true)

        val voices = listOf(

```kotlin
import com.google.android.gms.common.api.ApiException

private lateinit var googleSignInClient: GoogleSignInClient

    .requestIdToken(getString(R.string.default_web_client_id))
    .requestEmail()
    .build()

private val signInLauncher = registerForActivityResult(
    ActivityResultContracts.StartActivityForResult()

    val task = GoogleSignIn.getSignedInAccountFromIntent(result.data)
    try {

}

private fun firebaseAuthWithGoogle(idToken: String) {
    val credential = GoogleAuthProvider.getCredential(idToken, null)
    auth.signInWithCredential(credential)
        .addOnCompleteListener(this) { task ->
            if (task.isSuccessful) {
                // Signed in with Firebase — proceed to token hand-off.
            }
        }
}
```

Goal: a user who signs in with **Firebase Auth** (Google or
Email/Password) can use **Supabase** (Postgres + RLS, Storage, Edge
Functions) as that signed-in user, with the Postgres role
**`authenticated`** — without migrating BADSHAH AI's backend off Supabase.

|---|---|

| Supabase URL | `https://aghlacmqlagmigoznxlm.supabase.co` |
| Firebase project | `badshah-ai-badshah222` (created 2026-11-15) |

There are two ways to do this. **Option A is the recommended one.** Option B

## Option A (RECOMMENDED) — Supabase Third-Party Auth (Firebase)

Supabase natively trusts Firebase as an external identity provider. The
client sends the **Firebase ID token** to Supabase; Supabase verifies it
against Google's published keys and treats the request as the
`authenticated` role. **No custom JWT minting, no shared secret, no Cloud
Function needed for the basic flow.**

### A.1 How validation works

- The Firebase ID token is a JWT with:
  - `iss` = `https://securetoken.google.com/badshah-ai-badshah222`
  - `aud` = `badshah-ai-badshah222`
  - `sub` = the Firebase UID
  - `exp` = at most 1 hour after issue
- Supabase fetches Google's JWKS (the signing keys for Secure Token) and
  verifies the signature, issuer, audience, and expiry on every request.
- Because the token is verified as an external provider token, PostgREST /
  Storage / Realtime apply RLS as the **`authenticated`** role, and SQL
  policies can read the token's claims with `auth.jwt()`.

### A.2 Dashboard steps  ·  PENDING (Supabase Dashboard, user account)

1. Open the Supabase Dashboard for project **`aghlacmqlagmigoznxlm`**
   (sign in as the project owner).
2. Go to **Authentication → Third-Party Auth** (in the Authentication
   section; on some dashboard versions it appears under
   **Authentication → Providers / Sign In / Third-Party**).
3. Add / enable **Firebase** as a third-party provider.
4. Enter the **Firebase Project ID** — the real value that replaces
   `badshah-ai-badshah222`. Nothing else is required: no secret, no key
   file. Supabase derives the issuer
   (`https://securetoken.google.com/<project-id>`) and JWKS endpoint from
   the Project ID.
5. Save. The change takes effect for new requests immediately; already

> If the Firebase entry is not visible in the dashboard, check the
> project's plan/feature availability in Supabase's Third-Party Auth docs

### A.3 Client side — pass the Firebase token to Supabase

**Android (Kotlin, supabase-ktx pattern):** configure the Supabase client
so every request carries the current Firebase ID token. The supabase-ktx
Auth plugin supports a custom access-token provider; conceptually:

```kotlin
// Pseudocode — wire to the exact supabase-ktx version used in the app.
val supabase = createSupabaseClient(SUPABASE_URL, SUPABASE_ANON_KEY) {
    install(Auth) {
        // Always return the *current* Firebase ID token.
        accessToken = {
            Firebase.auth.currentUser
                ?.getIdToken(false)?.await()?.token
        }
    }
    install(Postgrest)
    install(Storage)
}
```

Key points:

- `SUPABASE_URL` is `https://aghlacmqlagmigoznxlm.supabase.co`.
  `SUPABASE_ANON_KEY` refers to the project's anon/publishable key by name
  — it is public client configuration (it already ships in the web app);
  it grants nothing by itself once RLS is on. **Never** substitute the
  `service_role` key here.
- The token provider must return a **fresh** token: Firebase ID tokens
  expire after 1 hour and the SDK auto-refreshes them. Never cache a token
  string in SharedPreferences and reuse it across sessions.
- Sign-out must clear both sessions: `Firebase.auth.signOut()` and the
  Supabase client state.

**Web app (existing, supabase-js):** if the web app later adopts Firebase
sign-in too, the equivalent is creating the client with
`global: { headers / accessToken }` — supabase-js accepts an
`accessToken` callback returning the Firebase ID token, used instead of a
Supabase-issued session token. The current web app uses native Supabase
Auth and does not need this change today.

**Direct REST calls:** send both headers —

```
apikey: <anon/publishable key>
Authorization: Bearer <Firebase ID token>
```

### A.4 RLS — using the token in policies

With Third-Party Auth, inside Postgres/RLS:

- `auth.jwt()` returns the **Firebase token's claims** (decoded JWT).
- `auth.role()` resolves to `'authenticated'` for a valid Firebase token.
- The Firebase UID is available as `auth.jwt() ->> 'sub'`
  (also mirrored in the standard `user_id` claim Supabase exposes for
  third-party tokens — verify against your Supabase version's docs).

Example policy pattern — a row owned by the Firebase user:

```sql
-- Table public.user_data has a column firebase_uid text.
create policy "users manage their own rows"
on public.user_data
for all
to authenticated
using  ( firebase_uid = (auth.jwt() ->> 'sub') )
with check ( firebase_uid = (auth.jwt() ->> 'sub') );
```

Migration warning: existing BADSHAH AI tables keyed by Supabase
`auth.users.id` (UUID) will **not** match Firebase UIDs automatically.
Rows created under Supabase Auth and rows created under Firebase Auth are
different identities until an explicit account-linking step maps them.
Design new Firebase-side tables around the Firebase UID (`sub`), and do
not silently mix the two identity spaces in one policy.

### A.5 Custom claims and the `role: 'authenticated'` requirement

Firebase ID tokens do not contain a Supabase `role` claim by default —
under Option A they don't need to: Supabase assigns the `authenticated`
role because the token comes from a trusted third-party provider.

If any part of the stack (an Edge Function, a custom PostgREST setup, or
Option B below) inspects the token directly, the expected claim shape is:

```json
{
  "role": "authenticated",
  "supabase_role": "authenticated",
  "firebase_uid": "<Firebase UID — same value as sub>",
  "sub": "<Firebase UID>",
  "aud": "authenticated",
  "iss": "https://aghlacmqlagmigoznxlm.supabase.co/auth/v1",
  "exp": 0
}
```

How to read this shape:

- `role: "authenticated"` — the Postgres role PostgREST switches to.
  In Option A this is conferred by Supabase; in Option B it must be
  inside the minted token (see B.3). The Cloud Function
  `setSupabaseClaims` in `../functions/` also stamps
  `role` + `supabase_role` as **Firebase custom claims**, so they appear
  inside the Firebase ID token itself after a forced token refresh —
  useful for any component that reads Firebase claims directly.
- `firebase_uid` — convenience copy of the UID for claim-based policies.
- `sub` — the subject. For Supabase-issued semantics this is the user ID;
  in Option B it is set to the Firebase UID.
- `aud: "authenticated"` — required audience for Supabase-compatible
  tokens (Option B). (In Option A, the Firebase token's own `aud` is the
  Firebase Project ID — that is correct and expected; do not confuse the
  two audiences.)
- `iss` — Option B issuer is `<Supabase URL>/auth/v1`. In Option A the
  issuer stays `https://securetoken.google.com/badshah-ai-badshah222`.
- `exp` — must be in the future and **≤ 1 hour** from issue for minted
  tokens (Option B); Firebase's own tokens already satisfy this.

Setting the Firebase custom claims (both options can use this):

1. Deploy the functions in `../functions/` (needs Blaze — Doc 05).
2. From the app, after sign-in, call the HTTPS callable
   **`setSupabaseClaims`** once. It requires `request.auth` and sets
   `{ role: 'authenticated', supabase_role: 'authenticated' }` on the
   caller via the Admin SDK.
3. In the app, call `getIdToken(true)` to force-refresh so the new claims
   are visible in `result.claims`.
4. New users can receive the same claims automatically via the
   `beforeUserCreated` identity blocking function in the same package —
   blocking functions must additionally be enabled in the Firebase
   Console (Authentication → Settings → Blocking functions). Treat that
   hook as a convenience; the callable remains the reliable path if the
   hook is not enabled.

## Option B (FALLBACK) — Custom-minted Supabase JWT via Cloud Function

Use **only** if Option A is unavailable for this project (plan/feature
limits) or a component strictly requires a Supabase-shaped token.

### B.1 How it works

The callable function **`mintSupabaseToken`** in `../functions/`:

1. Verifies the caller is signed in (`request.auth` — a valid Firebase
   token checked by the Functions runtime/Admin SDK).
2. Reads the **Supabase JWT secret** from
   `process.env.SUPABASE_JWT_SECRET` (populated from **Firebase Secret
   Manager** — see B.2). If the variable is missing, the function throws
   a clear error and mints nothing.
3. Signs a short-lived JWT (HS256, `jsonwebtoken`) with:

```json
{
  "role": "authenticated",
  "sub": "<Firebase UID>",
  "aud": "authenticated",
  "iss": "https://aghlacmqlagmigoznxlm.supabase.co/auth/v1",
  "exp": "<now + max 1 hour>",
  "firebase_uid": "<Firebase UID>",
  "email": "<user email, if present>"
}
```

4. The client uses that JWT as the Supabase `Authorization: Bearer` token
   (with the anon key as `apikey`) until it expires, then calls the
   function again. `auth.jwt()` in RLS sees these claims; `sub` is the
   Firebase UID.

### B.2 Secret handling — non-negotiable

- The Supabase JWT secret is found in Supabase Dashboard →
  **Project Settings → API → JWT Settings** (owner account only).
- Store it **only** in Firebase Secret Manager and bind it to the
  function, e.g.:

  ```bash
  firebase functions:secrets:set SUPABASE_JWT_SECRET
  ```

  (The CLI prompts for the value; it is never typed into source code.)
- The secret value must **never** appear in: source code, this package,
  the final ZIP, Git history, client apps, logs, or chat. Whoever holds
  it can mint a token for **any** user with **any** role — treat it like
  the `service_role` key.
- Record in `../PROJECT-VALUES.md` only *that* the secret was set and
  when — never its value.

### B.3 Risks vs Option A

- **Blast radius:** a leaked JWT secret = full impersonation of any user.
  Option A has no shared secret at all.
- **Upkeep:** token minting, refresh timing, and clock skew are your
  problem; Option A reuses Firebase's 1-hour token lifecycle.
- **Revocation:** a minted token stays valid until `exp` even if the
  Firebase account is disabled in the meantime (keep `exp` short).
- **Rotation:** rotating the Supabase JWT secret invalidates all minted
  tokens and requires updating Secret Manager.

## Decision summary

| | Option A — Third-Party Auth | Option B — Minted JWT |
|---|---|---|
| Recommended | ✅ Yes | Fallback only |
| Shared secret | None | Supabase JWT secret (Secret Manager only) |
| Cloud Function needed | Only for custom claims (optional) | Yes — `mintSupabaseToken` |
| Token used with Supabase | Firebase ID token itself | Minted Supabase-shaped JWT |
| `role: authenticated` from | Supabase trusts the provider | `role` claim inside minted token |
| RLS identity (`sub`) | Firebase UID | Firebase UID |

# 04 — SHA Fingerprints (SHA-1 / SHA-256)

App: **BADSHAH AI** · Package: `dev.pages.badshah222ai`

## The real fingerprints for the current APK

These come from the **signing certificate of the user's real APK**
(`Badshah222-ai.apk`) — the key the currently distributed app is signed
with. They are the fingerprints that must be registered in Firebase for
the installed app to pass Google Sign-In and related checks.

```
SHA-1:   D3:B2:3F:C1:B8:E1:16:59:9B:D0:C0:17:44:A8:1B:7A:A2:4B:62:F5
SHA-256: 6D:81:F8:E8:58:9D:A2:67:11:5D:B2:7D:16:48:B1:34:B7:39:F0:1D:9E:6E:19:05:C9:7C:5A:0E:22:46:DF:FD
```

- **SHA-1 is mandatory** for Firebase Authentication with the **Google**
  provider. Without it, Google Sign-In fails on device (often error 10,
  "developer error").
- SHA-256 is used by newer Google Play services / app-link and integrity
  features — register both.
- `MainActivity` in this APK is `com.atriidev.clientthinapp.MainActivity`
  (the app was produced with a client-app builder). That does **not**
  change the package name or the fingerprints: Firebase cares about the
  package (`dev.pages.badshah222ai`) + signing certificate pair.

## Where to add them in the Firebase Console

1. Console → **⚙ Project settings → General → Your apps** → select the
   Android app `dev.pages.badshah222ai`.
2. Under **SHA certificate fingerprints**, click **Add fingerprint**.
3. Paste the SHA-1, save. Repeat for the SHA-256.
   (SHA-1 can also be entered during the initial app registration —
   Doc 01 Step 2.)
4. After adding a fingerprint, **re-download `google-services.json`** and
   replace the file in `app/` — the OAuth client entries inside it are
   generated from the registered fingerprints.

A single app entry can hold **multiple** fingerprints — you will need
that, because debug, release, and Play keys are all different (below).

## Getting fingerprints for other keys (keytool)

Use these when new builds are signed with different keys. `keytool`
ships with the JDK. The output lines are labelled `SHA1:` and `SHA256:`.

### Debug key (local development builds)

Default debug keystore (password `android`, alias `androiddebugkey`):

```bash
# Linux/macOS
keytool -list -v -keystore ~/.android/debug.keystore -alias androiddebugkey -storepass android -keypass android

# Windows
keytool -list -v -keystore "%USERPROFILE%\.android\debug.keystore" -alias androiddebugkey -storepass android -keypass android
```

Or from Gradle (prints both MD5/SHA-1/SHA-256 per variant):

```bash
./gradlew signingReport
```

### Release key (your own upload/release keystore)

```bash
keytool -list -v -keystore /path/to/release.keystore -alias <your-alias>
```

You will be prompted for the keystore password. Use the fingerprints from
the `SHA1:` / `SHA256:` lines exactly as printed.

### From an already-built APK/AAB (no keystore needed)

This is how the fingerprints at the top of this document were verified
for the distributed APK:

```bash
keytool -printcert -jarfile Badshah222-ai.apk
```

## Play App Signing — important if the app is published on Google Play later

The APK covered by this package is **direct-distributed** (installed
outside Google Play) and signed with the builder's key — the fingerprints
above belong to that key.

If BADSHAH AI is later published through **Google Play**:

- Google re-signs the app with the **Play App Signing key**, which has
  **different** SHA-1/SHA-256 fingerprints.
- Those Play fingerprints must **also** be added to the same Firebase app
  entry, or Google Sign-In (and other fingerprint-checked features) will
  work in direct installs but **fail for Play installs**.
- Find them in **Play Console → your app → Test and release → App
  integrity (Play App Signing) → App signing key certificate** — copy the
  SHA-1 and SHA-256 shown there into Firebase (Project settings → Your
  apps → Add fingerprint), then re-download `google-services.json`.
- The **upload key** certificate shown on the same Play page is a third
  key; its fingerprints are needed for some upload-related flows, not for
  end-user sign-in. Register the *app signing* key for Firebase Auth.

## Rules

- Never invent, trim, or "tidy up" a fingerprint — copy it character for
  character, colons included (the console also accepts it without colons,
  but exact copy avoids mistakes).
- Every distinct signing key that end users install builds from needs its
  fingerprints registered: **builder/release key (done — above), debug
  key (for dev builds), Play App Signing key (if/when on Play).**
- Removing a fingerprint from the console breaks sign-in for builds
  signed with that key. Add first, test, then clean up.

create or replace function public.verify_admin_password(
    p_password text
)
returns boolean
language plpgsql
security definer
set search_path = ''
as $$
declare
    stored_hash text;
begin
    if p_password is null
       or length(p_password) < 1
       or length(p_password) > 256 then
        return false;
    end if;

    select password_hash
    into stored_hash
    from private.admin_credentials
    where id = 1;

    if stored_hash is null then
        return false;
    end if;

    return extensions.crypt(p_password, stored_hash) = stored_hash;
end;
$$;

revoke all on function public.verify_admin_password(text)
from public, anon, authenticated;

grant execute on function public.verify_admin_password(text)
to service_role;

-- Called only by authenticated server-side admin code.

create or replace function public.change_admin_password(
    p_new_password text
)
returns boolean
language plpgsql
security definer
set search_path = ''
as $$
begin
    if p_new_password is null
       or length(p_new_password) < 12
       or length(p_new_password) > 256 then
        return false;
    end if;

    update private.admin_credentials
    set password_hash = extensions.crypt(
        p_new_password,
        extensions.gen_salt('bf', 12)
    ),
    updated_at = now()
    where id = 1;

    return found;
end;
$$;

# Admin guide

URL: `https://YOUR-DOMAIN.com/admin` · password only, no username or email, no public registration.

## Login and security
* Password is checked in the database against a **bcrypt** hash (cost 12). The hash and the password never reach the browser.
* After 5 wrong attempts from one network (or 40 overall) in 15 minutes, logins are refused with a lock-out message, even for the right password.
* The session token lives in an **HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Strict** cookie that page JavaScript cannot read. It expires after inactivity (30 min) and after a maximum lifetime (2 h). **Sign out** revokes it on the server.
* The dashboard's files are served only to a valid session (checked server-side by the Worker); unauthenticated visitors are redirected.
* All changes (block, delete, reply, config...) are written to the audit log.

## Sections
1. **Overview**: users, active 24h/7d/30d, new sign-ups, AI requests (24h/7d/30d/all), Gemini vs Groq, conversations, messages, open tickets, 30-day chart.
2. **Users**: search, filter active/blocked, ID (Firebase UID), email (when the user's account has one), registration, last login/activity, provider/model, API-key-configured yes/no, voice. Click a row to edit the display name, **Block / Unblock**, or **Delete** (you must type the exact user ID).
3. **Login analytics**: successful logins, registrations, by provider, recent events. Failed logins appear only if the app reports them; Firebase rejects bad passwords before Supabase sees them.
4. **API analytics**: per provider/model requests, success/failure, average latency, token counts (when the provider returns them), top error codes, daily chart.
5. **Support center**: all tickets, read, **reply** (shown in the user's app and emailed if email is configured), change status, resolve.
6. **App management**: maintenance notice, announcements, server voice presets, non-secret app config (keys that look like secrets are refused).
7. **Security**: change password, active sessions (revoke), login history, audit log.

## What admins can never see
Users' API keys (they are not stored anywhere on the server) and chat text (no admin function returns it). The user detail view shows counts and provider *status* only.

## Daily use tips
* Prefer **Block** to **Delete**: deleting does not remove the Firebase login.
* If email shows "skipped", set `RESEND_API_KEY` and `EMAIL_FROM` (SUPABASE-SETUP.md).

# AI and voice provider setup (for users)

BADSHAH AI ships with **no API key**. Every person enters their own. Keys are stored encrypted (Android Keystore) on that phone only; they are never sent to BADSHAH servers, and the admin panel cannot see them.

## Google Gemini
1. Open https://aistudio.google.com/app/apikey and sign in.
2. Create an API key, copy it.
3. App → Settings → AI brain → **Google Gemini** → paste → **Test & save**. The app calls Google's model list with your key; a real answer proves it works.
4. Pick a model from the list that Google returns for *your* key.

## Groq
1. Open https://console.groq.com/keys, create a key, copy it.
2. Settings → AI brain → **Groq** → paste → Test & save → pick a model.

You can switch provider any time; each provider keeps its own key and model.

## ElevenLabs (optional)
Works independently of Gemini/Groq and costs ElevenLabs credits.
1. https://elevenlabs.io/app/settings/api-keys → create key.
2. Settings → ElevenLabs → paste → Test & save → choose a voice → switch the Voice engine to ElevenLabs.
If ElevenLabs fails (quota, network) the app tells you and speaks with the phone voice instead.

## Error messages you may see
| Message | Meaning |
|---|---|
| "rejected this API key" | Wrong/revoked key. Create a new one. |
| "too many requests / quota" | Free limit reached. Wait or switch provider. |
| "model is not available" | Pick another model after Test & save. |
| "No internet connection" | Phone offline or provider unreachable. |

## Male voices (honest behaviour)
Android's text-to-speech API does **not** report a voice's gender. The app lists the real voices installed on the phone, marks as MALE only those whose engine name says so, and shows the rest as "unverified" so you can preview them. The styles Deep / Natural / Professional / Friendly / Calm / Cinematic change pitch and speed of the voice you chose; they are not separate voices. Urdu, Hindi and Pashto appear only if the phone actually has them (Settings shows installed or not; Pashto is rare). Use **Install voice data** to add more, or ElevenLabs.

* New tables `voice_profiles` and `email_outbox`; support-ticket triggers; seed rows in `app_config`.

## 5. Email notifications

Replies are always saved in the app. Email is sent through [Resend](https://resend.com) when `RESEND_API_KEY` and `EMAIL_FROM` are set (use an address on a domain you verified there; no address is assumed). If not configured, the admin sees `Email skipped: ...` and the row is recorded in `email_outbox`. It is never reported as sent when it was not.

## Row Level Security summary

Every public table has RLS. A user can read/write only rows where `user_id = auth.jwt()->>'sub'` (their Firebase UID). Clients cannot insert login events or usage rows directly; they must use the validated functions. Admin functions are executable by `service_role` only. All of this is covered by 56 automated checks in `backend/supabase/tests/run-migrations-and-rls.mjs`.

# Troubleshooting

## Build
| Problem | Fix |
|---|---|
| `google-services.json` missing / package mismatch | File must be at `android-app/app/google-services.json` and contain package `dev.pages.badshah222ai`. |
| `default_web_client_id` unresolved | The Google Services plugin generates it from `google-services.json`; the file needs an OAuth client of type 3 (web). Re-download it after enabling Google sign-in. |
| Gradle / AGP version errors | Use JDK 17. The project pins Gradle 8.10.2, AGP 8.7.3, Kotlin 2.0.21, Compose BOM 2024.12.01. |
| A Kotlin compile error on first build | The Android code could not be compiled where it was written (no SDK). Send the exact error text to support; typical fixes are one-line import changes. |
| Release APK will not install | It is `UNSIGNED`. Add signing secrets or `keystore.properties`. |

## App
| Problem | Fix |
|---|---|
| "Cloud sync is off" banner | Firebase function `setSupabaseClaims` is not deployed (needs Blaze plan), or Supabase Third-Party Auth for project `badshah-ai-badshah222` is off, or migration 002 is not applied. Local chat still works. |
| Google sign-in fails with "no credential" / error 10 / 16 | SHA-1 of the signing key not registered in Firebase, or no Google account on the phone. |
